extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, historians of mathematics, students and general readers interested in the social/historical/philosophical aspects of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpted chapter discussing the social, political, ethical, and practical roles of mathematics (pure vs applied), with historical examples (Hardy, Maoist China, commerce, war, mysticism, astrology). Useful for readers exploring how external forces and values shape mathematical activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardyism (pursue 'useless' mathematics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardyism is the doctrine that one ought only to pursue useless mathematics. This doctrine is given as a purely personal credo in Hardy's A Mathematician’s Apology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a personal, aesthetic/ethical credo valuing pure, abstract mathematics for its own sake rather than social utility. No scoring guidance; functions as a philosophical stance about the desirable direction of mathematical research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Maoism (pursue socially useful mathematics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical Maoism is the doctrine that one ought to pursue only those aspects of mathematics which are socially useful. 'The first demand is production.' Research should serve proletarian politics, serve the workers, peasants and the soldiers and be integrated with productive labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes concrete policy manifestations: review committees to assess importance of fields, directing research toward practical problems, teaching based on concrete applications, and pressuring researchers to abandon some areas (e.g., topology). Emphasizes practical production and social utility as primary evaluative criteria for mathematical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production-first criterion (prioritize production over aesthetic arguments)
rubrics_metrics.description: In dialogues with Chinese mathematicians the answer to whether to present the beauty of mathematics was: 'The first demand is production.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to justify emphasizing industrially relevant problems (water and gas pipes, rolling mills, cables) over abstract notions of beauty; suggests that production and tangible contributions to society can be prioritized when assessing what mathematics should be taught or researched.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between beauty and utility
rubrics_metrics.description: What one wants to achieve, of course, in mathematics as well as in life in general, is a balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly posed as an evaluative ideal—research and teaching should find an appropriate balance between aesthetic/abstract aims and practical/social usefulness. The text questions whether a proper balance exists and notes historical imbalances (e.g., 'Mathematical Maoism' excess) and corrective measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-in-one principle (integration of social strata in research)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research was supposed to combine the efforts of the administrators, the researchers and the workers, the old, the middle-aged, and the young. This is known as the 'three-in-one' principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A procedural/political rubric for organizing scientific work: interdisciplinary and cross-class collaboration and mixing of ages/roles are treated as desirable for socially directed research; implies evaluation of projects on how well they integrate these groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political/procedural assessment of research importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Review committees were supposed to assess the importance of fields and subfields, keeping in mind the criterion that research should be directed towards practical problems and that teaching should be based upon concrete applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies an administrative rubric whereby the societal/practical importance of a field is the key metric for resource allocation and permissible research directions; used to justify large-scale redirection of scientific priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical evaluation of institutional association (contamination by military/government support)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many opponents of the war considered it immoral to work in military-supported institutions. It no longer mattered if one was working on military or nonmilitary problems; the whole institution was regarded as contaminated by evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides an ethical criterion for evaluating where (and whether) to do research: institutional funding/source and mission can render the work morally suspect. Cited consequences include protests, radical actions against institutions, and personal decisions to renounce government support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral responsibility of scientists and mathematicians
rubrics_metrics.description: With the development of weapons (e.g., the atomic bomb) mathematicians and physicists experienced a sense of sin; mathematics was seen as capable of doing physical, social, and psychological damage. Some compartmentalized mathematics into 'good' (pure) and 'bad' (applied) parts or renounced certain support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as an evaluative stance: the moral consequences of one's work and its possible harmful uses should be part of how one judges or chooses research. Includes examples of personal repudiation of certain kinds of funding or problem domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence standards for historical technical practices (e.g., astrology)
rubrics_metrics.description: To practise astrology in its intensive forms, one had to know astronomy, mathematics, medicine and much besides, for its methods (algorithms) were elaborate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes an implicit rubric for legitimacy/practice: historically, interdisciplinary technical competence (mathematics/astronomy/medicine) was required to perform certain applied or proto-scientific activities; emphasizes that technical rigor and requisite knowledge were part of practice even when underlying theory was mistaken.
